blurb: Google's TPU, big tech's own chips, speed-obsessed startups, and the little AI engine inside your phone.

cards.title: A chip built for one job

steps.p: Around 2013 Google calculated that if people used voice search for a few minutes a day, running the neural networks could mean doubling its data centers.
So Google designed the TPU — a chip that does almost nothing except the matrix maths neural networks need, and does it very efficiently.
steps.analogy: A GPU is a Swiss Army knife; a TPU is a very sharp chef's knife.

steps.p: Inside is a grid of thousands of tiny multiply-add units. Numbers pulse through the grid, each unit passing results to its neighbour — so data is reused instead of fetched again from memory.

items: Numbers enter one edge of the grid
Each unit multiplies, adds, passes on
Results flow out the other edge

steps.p: TPUs are linked into "pods" of thousands of chips with fast custom connections, acting like one giant computer.
You can't buy TPUs for your own servers. You rent them through Google Cloud — Google keeps the hardware.

cards.q: What drove Google to start the TPU project?
options: A forecast that neural networks like speech recognition could otherwise need double the data centers
Its phones running out of battery
cards.why: A cost crisis. Building a custom chip was cheaper than building a second set of data centers.

cards.q: Why is a systolic array efficient for matrix maths?
options: Numbers are reused as they flow between neighbouring units, avoiding repeated trips to memory
It runs at a higher temperature
It uses light instead of electricity
cards.hint: Look at the flow in step 3.
cards.why: Reuse, not re-fetch. Fetching from memory costs far more energy than the maths itself, so passing numbers along is a big win.

cards.statement: The first TPU was designed only for running models, not for training them.
cards.why: True. Version 1 (in use from 2015) only served models. Later generations added training.

cards.title: Google's Ironwood TPU (2025) was its first designed mainly for running models at scale — in pods of 9,216 chips.
cards.detail: Google called it built for the "age of inference": answering users' questions, especially with reasoning models, now takes more computing than training.

cards.statement: You can buy Google's data-center TPUs to install in your own servers.
cards.why: False. They're only available to rent through Google Cloud. That's a key difference from NVIDIA, which sells to everyone.

steps.p: Amazon (Trainium, Inferentia), Microsoft (Maia), Meta (MTIA) and Google (TPU) all design AI chips for their own data centers.
NVIDIA's GPUs are expensive and in short supply. A chip tuned to your own workloads can be cheaper per answer and reduce dependence on one supplier.
steps.analogy: A restaurant chain growing its own vegetables instead of paying a single supplier's prices.

steps.p: AMD's MI300X competes directly with NVIDIA, with more memory per chip — useful for holding big models.
Cerebras makes one chip the size of a whole silicon wafer, keeping enormous amounts of memory right on the chip.
NVIDIA's real advantage is CUDA — years of software, tools and know-how built around its chips. Switching takes work.

cards.q: Amazon's custom chip for training AI models is called…
cards.why: Trainium. Its sibling Inferentia focuses on running models. Graviton is Amazon's general-purpose CPU.

cards.statement: Anthropic uses Amazon's Trainium chips to train models.
cards.why: True. As part of Amazon's investment, Anthropic trains on large Trainium clusters such as Project Rainier, alongside other hardware.

cards.title: Cerebras builds a single chip the size of an entire silicon wafer.
cards.detail: Its Wafer Scale Engine 3 covers about 46,000 mm² with around 4 trillion transistors — roughly 50 times the area of a large GPU.

cards.statement: AMD's MI300X carries more high-bandwidth memory than NVIDIA's H100.
cards.why: True. 192 GB versus 80 GB, so a big model can fit on fewer chips.

cards.q: What's the biggest obstacle for NVIDIA's competitors?
options: How mature and familiar NVIDIA's software is
NVIDIA's chips are the only ones that work
cards.why: Software habits. Most AI code assumes CUDA. Rival chips can be fast, but moving code and tools over costs time and money.

steps.p: GPUs are flexible: training, serving, graphics, science. Flexibility costs some efficiency.
Startups like Groq and Cerebras build chips just for running models, aiming for very fast replies.
Groq spreads a model across many chips and keeps its numbers in super-fast on-chip memory (SRAM), avoiding slow trips to separate memory.

right.title: HBM (beside chip)
points: Much bigger and cheaper per byte

steps.p: A chip built for one task is usually more efficient — but if the task changes, it may be stuck.
steps.analogy: A pizza oven makes perfect pizza fast; a normal oven can cook anything.

steps.p: These startups bet that serving AI will be a huge market and that today's model designs are stable enough to build for.

cards.q: Groq's chips get much of their speed by keeping the model's numbers in…
options: Fast on-chip memory spread across many chips
cards.hint: Look at the comparison in step 3.
cards.why: On-chip SRAM. No waiting for separate memory means very fast replies — but it takes many chips to fit one model.

cards.statement: A chip designed only to run transformers would struggle if the main AI design changed.
cards.why: True. That's the risk of specialising. GPUs adapt to new designs; a fixed-purpose chip may not.

cards.q: Compared with a GPU, a chip designed for one fixed task is usually…
cards.why: Efficient but narrow. No wasted circuitry, but no room for other jobs.

cards.title: Groq was founded by Jonathan Ross, who worked on the original Google TPU.
cards.detail: Many AI chip startups trace back to the TPU team, which proved custom chips for neural networks could beat general-purpose hardware.

cards.q: Why don't all chips just use SRAM instead of HBM?
options: SRAM holds far less per chip and costs much more per byte
cards.why: Density and cost. SRAM is fastest, but you'd need hundreds of chips to hold a big model.

cards.title: The AI engine in your pocket

steps.p: Modern phone and laptop chips include an NPU — a small section built just for AI maths, sitting beside the CPU and GPU.
Running on your device is private (data stays put), works offline, responds instantly and saves battery compared with general-purpose chips.
Face unlock, photo enhancement, live captions, voice typing and small on-device chatbots all use the NPU.
NPUs are rated in TOPS — trillions of operations per second. Microsoft requires 40+ for its Copilot+ PC label.
steps.analogy: Like horsepower for car engines: a rough guide, not the full story.

steps.p: Apple's Neural Engine first appeared in the iPhone X's A11 chip in 2017. Now nearly every new phone has one.

cards.q: Microsoft's Copilot+ PC label requires an NPU of at least…
cards.why: 40 TOPS. Enough to run features like live translation and image tools locally.

cards.statement: Apple's Neural Engine first appeared in the A11 chip in the iPhone X in 2017.
cards.why: True. It powered Face ID and camera features from day one.
Trillions of operations per second. A rough measure of peak speed — real performance also depends on memory and software.

cards.title: Face ID matches your face entirely on the iPhone, never sending it to Apple's servers.
cards.detail: The Neural Engine compares a depth map of your face with a stored mathematical representation, all on the device — a privacy benefit of local AI.

cards.title: Find your laptop's NPU
cards.body: On Windows, Task Manager's Performance tab shows an NPU if your computer has one. On a Mac, every Apple-chip model has a Neural Engine.
cards.challenge: Check whether your laptop or phone has an NPU, and look up its TOPS rating.
